abstract: Proactive management of invasive species aims to prevent and eradicate new incursions before they establish. Genomic data can assist proactive management around how to deploy resources and when to change strategies, and has been used effectively in managing Aedes albopictus (Asian tiger mosquito) in the Australian Northern Peninsula Area over the past decade. This study characterises the first major incursion of Ae. albopictus on the Australian mainland, and contrasts this with long-term genomic monitoring of this species within the Torres Strait Islands (TSI). First, we genomically traced the mainland incursion, which was detected in Cape York, Queensland, to the nearest infested island, Muralug (Prince of Wales). Strong genetic drift patterns in the incursion are suggestive of recent inbreeding, and point to a lag between incursion and detection of at least two mosquito generations. This stands in stark contrast with incursions within the TSI, which showed no evidence of inbreeding, suggesting no detection lag in the TSI. We genomically traced n=63 incursions detected in the TSI between 2019-2026, including n=44 newly sequenced samples; this used an expanded reference databank containing samples from one island, Muralug, that had not been available in previous tracing. Including Muralug greatly improved tracing success from ~50% to 77.8-92.1%. We observed no reduction in tracing success when whole genome and reduced representation sequencing datasets were combined in analysis, indicating composite approaches are viable. Together these findings demonstrate the value of genomic databanks for long-term incursion monitoring, provided these capture a sufficient proportion of genetic variation.
